Question: Let \(R\) be a square region and \(n \geq 4\) an integer. A point \(X\) in the interior of \(R\) is called \(n\)-ray partitional if there are \(n\) rays emanating from \(X\) that divide \(R\) into \(n\) triangles of equal area. How many points are \(100\)-ray partitional but not \(60\)-ray partitional?
Solution:
Scaling the square preserves equal-area partitions and gives a one-to-one correspondence between the possible points. We may therefore use the unit square and write \(X=(x,y)\), where \(0<x,y<1\). We will characterize the points for even \(n\), which covers both \(100\) and \(60\).

First, every square corner must lie on a dividing ray. A corner between two consecutive ray endpoints would make that piece have at least four vertices, unless the two rays were opposite and \(X\) lay on a side of a corner triangle. This exceptional case also fails for even \(n\). Rotate the square so the omitted corner is bottom left, and join it to \(X\), splitting the corner triangle into positive areas \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). All other pieces then have \(X\) as a vertex. The full triangles from \(X\) to the top and bottom sides have areas summing to \(1/2\). The top triangle consists of whole pieces, while the bottom consists of whole pieces plus one of \(\alpha,\beta\). Since \(1/2=(n/2)(1/n)\), that partial area must be an integer multiple of \(1/n\). Using the right and left sides forces the other partial area to be an integer multiple too. Their positive sum would be at least \(2/n\), contradicting the corner triangle's area \(1/n\).

The four corner rays split the square into four triangles with apex \(X\). Each must contain a whole number of the equal-area pieces. The bottom triangle has area \(y/2\), and the left triangle has area \(x/2\). Thus
\[
\frac{ny}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{nx}{2}
\]
must be integers. The top and right triangles have areas \((1-y)/2\) and \((1-x)/2\); their required counts are also integers because \(n\) is even.

These conditions are sufficient as well. For each side, let \(k\) be \(n\) times the area of its triangle with apex \(X\). This is a positive integer. Divide that side into \(k\) equal segments and draw rays to the division points and corners. The resulting triangles have equal bases and a common height on that side, so each has area \(1/n\). The four values of \(k\) sum to \(n\), producing exactly \(n\) triangles and \(n\) distinct boundary rays.

For \(n=100\), the coordinate conditions give
\[
x=\frac{i}{50},\qquad y=\frac{j}{50},
\qquad 1\le i,j\le49.
\]
There are therefore \(49^2\) such points.

For a coordinate also to be allowed when \(n=60\), it must have both forms \(i/50\) and \(a/30\). Equality gives \(3i=5a\), so \(i=5k\), \(a=3k\), and the common coordinate is \(k/10\). The strict interior bounds give \(1\le k\le9\). Each coordinate thus has nine common possibilities, giving \(9^2\) points that satisfy both conditions.

Every grid point determines one location, and the common points are precisely those to exclude. The desired number is
\[
49^2-9^2=2401-81=\boxed{2320},
\]
which is choice C.
